messages.author: 7c8a33455cb7050c
messages.subject: Automating variogram interpretation
parts:
Hi, 

I'm working with a large boreal caribou telemetry dataset and am trying to compute adke annual home range estimates;   I have ~1000 caribou years to work with!  

Is there a way to automate the visual inspection of each caribou years variogram? 

Thus far, I skipped this step by using ctmm.guess and ctmm.select to fit a model, and then akde to compute a home range.  However, how meaningful is that home range size if the animal is not range resident (or at least the data isn't saying its range resident).  

For example, this is the variogram for one caribou year where the ou model was fit, and a home range was computed.  However, looking at this, I don't think an asymptote was reached, indicating the animal wasn't range resident and likely should be discarded from the analysis.  

My conclusion is that I can't skip the visual inspection.  However, with so much data (I know, don't complain, it's the holy grail), I'm keen to automate this!  Thoughts?  

Robin

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Automating variogram interpretation
parts:
Hi Robin,

We are working on a manuscript covering this issue right now. For the moment, I would consider a couple of options:
  1. In his comparative analysis, Mike looked at overlap estimates between home ranges estimated from the first half of the data and from the second half of the data, and applied a subjective overlap threshold to classify resident and non-resident: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ecm.1344
  2. New for the upcoming manuscript, I've implemented a ranging area cluster() function that will objectively classify area estimates into two groups—small (resident) and large (non-resident)—using a hierarchical mixture model.
  3. You might also consider applying a threshold DOF['area'] value. One-off migrations and dispersals will have a DOF['area'] of around 1, which is much less than the number of times an ungulate would tend to cross its home range over an extended period of time.
I would try sorting the output variogram comparisons (empirical versus theoretical) by one of these statistics (overlap, P(resident), DOF) and skimming through them to see which aligns more with your sense of the data.
In addition to variograms, I also find it useful to color the scatter plots by time, like

COL <- color(DATA,by='time')
plot(DATA,col=COL)

Best,
Chris
